rewrites.summary:
Spain is a very safe destination for transgender visitors. The 2023 "Trans Law" established legal gender recognition by self-identification and broad anti-discrimination protections, and a parallel penal-code reform made gender identity an explicit hate-crime ground — with real enforcement, including convictions carrying transphobia aggravation. There is no legal restriction on trans people using bathrooms or facilities matching their presentation, and the national tourism industry actively promotes Spain as an LGBTQ destination.

Acceptance is high in cities and tourist regions, though attitudes can be more conservative in some rural areas. Political debate around trans rights is heated, and some regional governments (Madrid, 2023) have rolled back regional protections — signals of a polarised climate rather than changes to a visitor's everyday legal position.

Documented incidents exist: harassment and verbal-abuse prosecutions, a high-profile local-police transphobia case in Benidorm, and gangs targeting queer tourists through dating apps (mainly gay men) in tourist zones — the latter being a general safety caution for app-based meetups anywhere.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Dating-app predation gangs in tourist zones (mainly targeting gay men) — a caution for trans visitors using apps.
rewrites.localsOnly: The 2023 Trans Law's self-identification LGR procedure is resident-facing administrative law.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Petty theft in tourist hotspots, drunken nightlife incidents, and general terrorism guidance affect all travellers. Dating-app meeting risks apply to everyone using them.

blindSourceSummaries: Official national-gazette text of the 2023 trans-equality law (28 February 2023): any person of legal age 16 or over may request rectification of the registry gender mention before the civil registry — the administrative self-identification route visitors and residents use; the law also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

An international human-rights organization (16 February 2023): parliament passed the trans-equality law — gender recognition now by self-identification through a simple administrative process, ending the prior requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. The law also expands assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans non-consensual 'normalising' surgeries on intersex children, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and adds anti-discrimination measures in healthcare, employment and housing; recognition possible from age 12 under conditions. A small group of countries have adopted similar recognition frameworks.

A national criminal-law firm analysis (June 2026): disentangles which statute does what — 'gender expression' appears in no article of the criminal code; the hate-speech aggravation (Article 22.4) and Article 510 penalties (1-4 years plus 6-12 month fine) come from a separate organic law (2022), while the 2023 law reformed offences against sexual freedom (Articles 132, 173, 178-181, 189 bis). Useful for reading actual enforcement: gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence.

An expat-news source (9 July 2026): practical bathroom-access contrast for travellers — a neighbouring country is moving toward stricter single-sex-space rules on biological-sex lines under an equality-body statutory code (restrictions case-by-case, not a blanket ban), while this country remains committed to a legal framework centred on gender self-determination. Visitor takeaway: facility access rules differ on either side of the border.

A travel company's country guide: rates this country a safe and welcoming destination for LGBTQIA+ travellers, especially tourist hubs in major cities, while noting attitudes can be more conservative outside big cities and that same-sex marriage plus protective laws apply. Advises knowing local conditions before going (venues, regional variation).

The national tourism institute's business page: this country as a reference destination for LGBTQ+ tourism — flagship destinations across major cities and resort areas, an annual Pride event at a resort, and an 'open and safe' certification for discrimination-free spaces. Practical destination map for trip planning.

A national newspaper (July 2026): a first-instance court applied the discrimination aggravating circumstance for transphobia, in a misdemeanour threats case — messages threatening a trans woman sent by a messaging app; the author was fined a few hundred euros. First instance-level precedent that gender-identity aggravation is being applied in practice.

An anti-hate-crime observatory report (8 January 2026): a youth gang in a park harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison, two minors were separately judged. Documents actual sentence outcomes for gender-identity-motivated violence.

A foreign government's travel advice for this country (safety and security): official view that the country is 'a generally tolerant and progressive place for LGBT+ travellers' with active communities and social venues, alongside standard crime warnings (counterfeit money treated as a serious offence). Baseline official safety framing for a foreign-issued passport holder.

Encyclopedia overview: same-sex marriage and full adoption rights since 2005; legal gender change without surgery or sterilisation; transgender military service and male same-sex blood donation since 2005; recognised as one of the world's most LGBT-friendly countries. Backbone timeline for the record.

A major news outlet's international 23-country public-opinion survey (December 2016): this country ranked the most trans-supportive of the 23 — the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change, restroom support over 70% (alongside two other surveyed countries), and 25% of respondents knew a trans person. Dated public-attitude baseline predating the 2023 law.
rewrites.notes: Named statute, cities and outlets genericised per rule 7b/7e; law dates, article numbers and penalties kept.

rewrites.summary:
Brazil combines some of the world's strongest legal protections for transgender people with a high level of real-world violence — the classic gap between law and practice. Courts allow name and gender-marker changes without surgery, the Supreme Court has criminalised transphobia (making it punishable like racism), courts fine businesses that discriminate, and official guidance affirms trans people's right to use bathrooms matching their identity.

For visitors, big-city queer life is vibrant and highly visible — São Paulo hosts the world's largest Pride parade — and the law is unambiguously on a trans traveller's side. The practical risks are concentrated in nightlife and app-based meetings: a majority of physical violence against LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo happens at night, and robbery schemes luring gay men via dating apps have been fatal.

Exercise particular caution after dark, with nightlife and app meetings, and in peripheral areas. Violence against local trans people (Brazil records the world's highest absolute toll) is heavily concentrated in poor and marginalised communities, not tourist areas.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Dating-app robbery schemes (documented as fatal for gay men) are a caution for trans visitors using apps.
rewrites.localsOnly: The name/gender-marker change procedure and the transphobia criminalisation are resident-facing legal machinery; the world's-highest trans murder toll falls on local trans people, concentrated in poor and marginalised communities.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Brazil's general crime problem (armed robbery, express kidnappings, gang violence) drives all governments to advise a high degree of caution for every traveller.

rewrites.summary:
Saudi Arabia is among the most dangerous countries in the world for a transgender person to be discovered in. Under its uncodified Sharia legal system, same-sex conduct is punishable in theory by death, flogging, or long imprisonment, and transgender expression itself is criminalised through "imitation of the opposite sex" and public-morality provisions that police and the morality police enforce with broad discretion. There is no legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care is banned.

Enforcement is documented and brutal: trans women have been arrested, detained, and tortured on morality grounds; a Pakistani trans woman died in custody in Riyadh in 2017 after a raid; men have been arrested for cross-dressing videos posted online. Amnesty International reported in 2026 that visitors have been imprisoned after unfair trials over social media posts — including posts published before they entered the Kingdom — and device inspection at the border is an established risk.

The tourism authority's "everyone is welcome" messaging reflects official interest in visitors' money, not any change in law. Any practical safety depends entirely on never being discovered, including digitally; detention would be in facilities matching passport sex, with no consular leverage able to prevent mistreatment.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct punishable in theory by death, flogging, or long imprisonment — a catastrophic formal exposure for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Missile and drone attacks on infrastructure, and the general risk of detention without charge for any visitor, affect all travellers.

An international human-rights organisation's country overview (updated 12 March 2026): criminal penalties are based on religious law; same-sex relations illegal for men and women; no legal gender recognition; LGBTI organisations cannot register anywhere in the country.

A regional legal-research institute's profile (trans archives): deviating from traditional gender norms is itself treated as a criminal offence; regional legal-research framing of gender-nonconformity provisions and their enforcement.

Encyclopedia 'LGBTQ rights in the country' article (fetched 2026): same-sex conduct illegal with penalties including capital punishment, indeterminate prison terms, flogging and fines; no gender-identity recognition, no discrimination protections, no same-sex relationship recognition; law uncodified on a conservative interpretation of religious sources, with enforcement-case and living-conditions sections. Reference overview.

A foreign public broadcaster: a trans woman from a neighbouring country died in custody after a roundup with 34 others in a prison, foreign activists say she was beaten with clubs, aggravating a chronic heart condition, while the national authorities attributed the death to a heart attack; family and trans-rights activists dispute the official account. Directly relevant to how enforcement here treats trans people.

A regional news outlet (25 October 2021): five men were arrested in a border region after filming themselves in women's clothing and posting the footage on social media — cross-dressing and gender-nonconformity enforced as a criminal matter.

An international human-rights organisation (29 June 2026, updated 17 July 2026): documents visitors imprisoned over social media posts — including a business analyst arrested at the main airport on 31 August 2024 as he was returning to another country with his family, targeted for posts published before he even arrived in the country. Enforcement reaches travellers for expression, not only conduct on the ground.

A foreign government's travel advice for this country (safety and security): same-sex relations are illegal although legal action is uncommon; couples should avoid public affection; the tourism authority states all visitors are welcome and privacy will be respected; being transgender is not recognised — trans travellers could face difficulties with dress codes and access to medical care.

An LGBTQ+ risk-map project (2024/25): this country appears among the least safe destinations for LGBTQ travellers in a ranking that also lists several other countries; the page also profiles the safest destinations (self-identification recognition, marriage equality since 2010).

rewrites.notes: Locations, organisations and religious-legal terms genericised; dates, penalties and enforcement facts kept; blindLocalsOnly omitted (source localsOnly null).

rewrites.summary:
Thailand is one of Asia's most accepting destinations for transgender visitors. Visible gender variance is part of mainstream culture (the kathoey tradition long predates modern categories), the state actively promotes LGBTQ tourism, same-sex marriage became legal in January 2025 as the first in Southeast Asia, and the Immigration Bureau runs a dedicated "Welcome Pride" initiative to smooth entry for travellers whose passports don't match their appearance or gender. Gender-affirming healthcare is a mature, accessible industry.

The gaps are legal rather than social: there is still no procedure to change one's legal gender marker, the 2015 Gender Equality Act is weakly enforced, and — as the 2025 murder of a Thai trans woman in Pattaya highlighted — Thailand has no hate-crime law, so bias-motivated violence is prosecuted as ordinary crime.

For a visitor the practical risks are mostly Thailand's general ones: nightlife disputes, scams, and alcohol-fuelled incidents, with some reported friction in resort nightlife districts. Everyday movement, hotels, healthcare, and transit are unproblematic.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Same-sex marriage legal since January 2025 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
rewrites.localsOnly: The absent legal gender marker procedure and the weakly enforced 2015 Gender Equality Act are resident-facing; the Pattaya murder and the hate-crime-law gap concern residents primarily.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Scams, drink-spiking in nightlife, road safety, and petty theft affect all travellers to Thailand.

blindSourceSummaries: A government public-relations page (5 August 2024): the immigration authority launched a welcome initiative to mitigate concerns of foreign LGBTQ+ travellers whose passports don't match their current appearance or gender — the entry-friction fix a trans visitor most needs to know about before arrival.

An international human-rights organisation's country overview (updated 12 March 2026): this country became the first in the region to legalise same-sex marriage — the bill passed its final parliamentary reading June 2024, in effect 22 January 2025, using gender-neutral 'marriage partners' terms; its at-a-glance tables also carry the legal-status read.

A local news outlet (2025) reporting on an advocacy forum: advocates urge the government to expedite a gender-recognition law following marriage equality, with public education framed as part of expanding rights protection — legal gender recognition is still pending after marriage equality.

A foundation news piece (November 2025): when a foreign tourist murdered a local trans woman in a resort town in April, the community called it a hate crime but the country's law has no hate-crime designation — bias-motivated violence is handled as an ordinary offence with no enhanced penalties or data collection; documents the accountability gap.

A local news outlet (5 May 2025): following the killing of a local trans woman by a foreign man after she refused his request for sex, LGBTQ+ groups urgently called for new hate-crime protections — documents the perpetrator and victim facts and the resulting legal-protection push.

An international human-rights organisation's report (December 2021): no route for transgender people to obtain legal documentation reflecting their gender identity; even affirmative measures like first-name change leave discretionary power with officials; anti-discrimination protections are not fully enforced — the documentation gap a trans visitor may also feel.

A foreign newspaper in English (May 2025): the conservative government introduced progressive trans laws including free hormone treatments with little public opposition; trans people report greater societal acceptance and higher company positions than typical elsewhere — explains why social climate outruns the legal framework.

A legal-information source (June 2026): marriage equality since January 2025 and anti-discrimination law since 2015, yet no mechanism to change the sex marker on birth certificate, national identification or passport (title prefixes locked to sex at birth; a 1962 name act as partial workaround) — precise current documentation-status read.

An analysis (June 2025): examines the government's push to position this country as an LGBTQ+ tourism hub (an annual Pride event as backdrop) alongside marriage equality — weighing opportunities and challenges of a government strategy whose motives range from genuine commitment to economic opportunism; relevant to how welcoming institutions are pitched to visitors.

A national law firm's analysis of the post-marriage-equality landscape: marriage equality closes practical gaps for couples — exclusion from property regimes, succession, hospital visitation and pension survivor claims — the concrete before/after of the January 2025 change.

An archive of local LGBT news (2007-10): the national human-rights commission's role, constitutional gay-rights campaigns, resort-area acceptance and rejection accounts, and a debate on trans legal titles — historical baseline showing how long recognition questions have been live.

rewrites.summary:
Mexico pairs meaningful legal progress with one of the world's highest tolls of violence against transgender people. Twenty-two of its 32 states offer administrative legal gender recognition, Mexico City and Nayarit have criminalised transfemicide, marriage equality is nationwide, and constitutional anti-discrimination protections exist.

Against that, 71 trans or gender-diverse people were murdered in a single recent year — the second-highest figure in the Americas after Brazil — with organised crime increasingly involved and impunity near-total. The victims are overwhelmingly local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit, not tourists; violence is also highly concentrated by region.

In major tourist destinations and central Mexico City, heavily policed and progressively governed, a trans visitor's everyday risk is closer to harassment than violence. The dominant hazard for any traveller is Mexico's general crime environment. Use the Admin Divisions view: state-level scores range from among Latin America's best (Mexico City) to levels comparable with its most dangerous regions.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Marriage equality nationwide — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
rewrites.localsOnly: The state-by-state administrative LGR regime and the transfemicide statutes (Mexico City, Nayarit) are resident-facing; the 71-murder toll falls overwhelmingly on local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Cartel violence, kidnapping, and theft drive several governments to advise caution or non-essential travel avoidance for parts of Mexico — a risk independent of any personal characteristic.

An international human-rights organisation's report (6 March 2024): barriers to legal name and gender recognition leave trans people exposed — document mismatch amplifies daily discrimination, against the backdrop of murders including a trans woman found in a river in August 2023.

A foreign newspaper (18 July 2024): the capital city's legislative body approved a transfemicide law — a watershed measure named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished; activists say the law is critical for feeling safe.

A news agency (January 2024): 'Wave of transgender killings spurs protests' — at least three transgender people killed in early 2024, including an activist shot in the capital, drawing LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests.

An intergovernmental human-rights body's press release (2024): urges national and regional authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanding investigation of all LGBTI violations with gender-identity-respecting methods; warns impunity may reach alarming levels.

A foreign government's travel advice for this country: 'Exercise a high degree of caution' nationwide due to high levels of criminal activity and kidnapping, with regional 'avoid non-essential travel' advisories in the most volatile border areas; recently updated for a hurricane.

Tour operator guide: same-sex marriage legalised in the country's capital in 2009 (the pioneer) with a gay district as its hub (annual Pride, LGBT-friendly hotels, bars and tours); a major beach resort is a mainstream hotspot; notes an indigenous third-gender tradition and advises caution outside tourist hubs.

A foreign-language news outlet (19 July 2024): the capital city's legislative body approved the transfemicide law; an international monitoring organisation records 593 transfemicides in the country between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023 — second only to another country's 100.

A foreign newspaper (13 January 2007): a state/province became the third jurisdiction in the region to approve same-sex civil unions (20-13 vote) after two other cities, barring adoption and custody for those couples; one legislator called it 'a sensible response' to discrimination, opponents called it an attack on the family.

rewrites.summary:
Brunei's Sharia Penal Code contains one of the world's most explicit trans-specific criminal provisions: Section 198 creates an offence of "a man posing as a woman or vice versa", and the Bruneian government has confirmed in its official guidance that the code applies to all persons in the country including tourists — travel agents are briefed accordingly. A separate indecency provision criminalises clothing that "tarnishes the image of Islam" with fines and imprisonment, and same-sex intimacy carries a stoning sentence (under a formal moratorium since 2019, with whipping and long prison terms actively available).

Enforcement is quiet rather than predatory — no prosecution of a foreign visitor under these provisions has been documented — but the country is an absolute monarchy with heavy surveillance, censorship, and no LGBT organising of any kind, and LGBT Bruneians have fled abroad. The legal exposure for a discovered trans visitor is categorical: no recognition, no protection, and gender expression itself is a written offence.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Same-sex intimacy carries a stoning sentence (moratorium since 2019, whipping and long prison terms available) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No current travel advisory flags general security risks; the hazards here are legal, not criminal.

An international human-rights organisation's global 'outlawed' map feature: at least 67 countries criminalise same-sex relations and at least nine criminalise forms of gender expression; this country is one of at least two whose national laws expressly criminalise 'posing as' or 'imitating' a person of a different sex — the record's trans-specific offence, alongside another country's analogue.

A foreign government's 2017 human-rights report on the country: the religious penal code bans men dressing as women or women dressing as men 'without reasonable excuse', with no known convictions in 2017; same-sex intimacy between men carries death by stoning if implemented, and the report records LGBTI-reported discrimination in employment, housing, recreation and services. Morality provisions (cross-dressing, alcohol, fasting and religious propagation) were enforced; implementing regulations were still unissued.
